statements.passage:
Artificial Intelligence and Programming

Programming languages were invented to allow humans to describe programs to
computers. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) now allow humans to describe
programs to computers in natural languages such as English. The programs
themselves are still written in programming languages and rely on the same
concepts and structures that they did prior to these AI advances. However, use
of AI tools to generate and manipulate programs is now pervasive.

CS 61A has been updated for the Fall 2026 offering to align with how programming
languages are now used in the AI era. After developing a comprehensive
understanding of programming, students will use AI coding agents in their final
project to develop a large and complex software application. The course includes
new content about software engineering and web technology. To make room, a few
topics that are also covered in CS 61B have been deferred to that later course.
See
What’s New
for more details.

Currently, the most capable users of AI for programming are those who have a
strong foundational understanding of programs and programming languages.
Effective use of AI, whether for programming or other domains, is enabled by
understanding precisely what outcome one desires and then being able to
describe it. Therefore, most of the content of the course has remained
unchanged in this update. Understanding programming well enough to read, write,
and manipulate programs, even without AI assistance, remains a core learning
goal of this course and a great use of students’ time.

statements.passage:
DANGER: LLMs are Prohibited from Accessing or Interacting with Code and Repositories

You must
never
allow an LLM or any GenAI tool to read, analyze, or interface with your codebase or your GitHub repository in any way. This means all local and terminal-based tools (e.g.,
Claude Code and Codex
), GitHub Copilot, built-in IDE extensions (e.g., Cursor, IntelliJ AI Assistant), or any other agentic coding tools are
outright banned
.

You may
ONLY
interact with LLMs and GenAI tools conceptually, and this interaction must take place
exclusively through browser-based chatbots
(such as chatgpt.com or claude.ai).

General Policy

Use LLMs in the same way you might use a friend in the class who is not in your group. You may only use browser-based chatbots to ask high-level, conceptual questions. You must
never
feed your code, skeleton code, or assignment instructions into an LLM, and no LLM-generated code should ever enter your codebase. As a general rule, no code or specific instructions from the course should be pasted, typed, or uploaded into an LLM. If at any point you find yourself stuck on an assignment, concept, or anything else related to CS 61B, we encourage you to find our staff at office hours or lab!

Code Interviews

In order to discourage unacceptable LLM use, we may be conducting random code interviews for all projects.

For students selected for code interviews, we’ll hold short interviews to verify that you are able to explain your code and are capable of generating similar code unassisted.

For more information, please see the
Code Interviews Policy
.

Question Types

The below policy applies to all interactions with LLMs relating to CS 61B content:

Reasonable Questions (Exclusively via browser-based chatbots)
:
These are things that are reasonable to ask an LLM:

“What’s the difference between Integer and int in Java?”

“What is a garbage collector?”

“What does this mean: Exception in thread “main” java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero”

Absolutely Forbidden
:
These questions/activities will massively detract from your learning experience in the course, and are strictly prohibited:

Allowing any LLM tool, IDE extension, or CLI assistant (e.g., Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, etc.) to access, read, run, or modify your code or repository.

Uploading or pasting your code, skeleton code, or errors from your project into an LLM.

“Write a snippet of code to make an array in Java.”

“Write a snippet of code to make every word uppercased in Jav

statements.anchor: the use of LLMs in this class is permitted with extreme caution for conceptual help only
statements.label: AI for conceptual questions only
statements.passage:
We believe that the most effective way to learn the course content is by engaging with it without the use of LLMs. If at any point you find yourself stuck on an assignment, concept, or anything else related to CS 61C, we encourage you to find our staff on Ed or office hours! That being said, the use of LLMs in this class is permitted with
extreme caution for conceptual help only
, and the below policy applies to all interactions with LLMs relating to CS 61C content:

Reasonable Questions.
These are things that are reasonable to ask an LLM.

"Why do we need to use pointers in C?"

"What is RISC-V Calling Convention?"

"What does the error message <C compiler error> mean?"

Unacceptable Uses of AI/Google/etc

"Here's the project prompt, please do it for me."

"Write this function for me."

"Here's my broken code, debug it for me."

It is
NOT OK
to use AI, Google, etc to complete work on Homework, Projects, and Labs.

NO AI help with coding is permitted in this course.

We believe that students are able to tell the difference between using an LLM to genuinely attempt to understand the course content more deeply and using an LLM to avoid engaging with the learning goals of the course / to complete assignments without learning more about the content. We also believe that LLMs are very prone to giving out incorrect answers, so we
will not
penalize asking about reasonable LLM output on course platforms. For example, if an LLM gives you information that seems to be wrong, please ask! We are here to support your learning and correct your misconceptions, and course staff is an official source of truth for 61C. It's better to ask us and be confident in the reply than to possibly internalize incorrect information after the end of this course.

Unless the instructions for a particular assignment state otherwise,
generative artificial intelligence tools that produce or revise text or
code, including ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and
similar tools, may be used for programming assignments. They may not be
used for the midterm or final exam.

The use of generative AI is permitted because learning to use such tools
critically and responsibly is relevant to professional work in computer
science. However, all use of generative AI must be honest, cited, and
documented.

If you use generative AI for a programming assignment, you must identify
and cite the tool or tools used and include a separate one-page AI usage
statement with your submission. The statement must:

identify the AI tool or tools used

explain specifically how each tool was used

summarize the relevant prompts or questions submitted to the tool

identify which parts of the submitted work were influenced by
AI-generated output

explain how the generated material was checked, corrected, or adapted

cite or acknowledge the generated material appropriately

Generative AI tools may fabricate information and may produce incorrect,
inefficient, insecure, or biased code or explanations. You are fully
responsible for the content and accuracy of everything you submit,
including work supported by generative AI.

You must understand your submitted code and be able to explain its
design, the algorithms and data structures used, its implementation,
correctness, running time, and any use of generative AI during its
development.

student's understanding of the submitted work. An inability to explain
submitted code may lead to further review of the student's work. Failure
to document AI use honestly may result in the matter being reported to the
Academic Integrity Office.

My understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their uses is
evolving. I think there's a chance that LLMs can be used as be powerful tools
in our search for knowledge and understanding. But it's also clear that they
can be used in ways that inhibit learning. I want to
develop course policies that will incentivize my students to
use LLMs only in the former ways rather than the latter. But for now I just
have a few general principles and a few case studies to offer as guidance.

First, some principles.

I am not going to prohibit the use of LLMs for this class, even though I
think such prohibitions are a reasonable choice at this moment.

Whenever you use text drawn verbatim or in summary form from another source,
you should cite that source. This includes LLMs.

Proper citation of an LLM's contributions includes quotation marks around
verbatim quotation, plus the name and version
of the specific LLM you used, as well as the
exact prompts you used to generate
the text you quoted or summarized
.

Properly quoting and citing an LLM's work will, in this course, prevent you
from violating Carleton's

academic integrity standards
;
it will not, however, prevent you from getting a low score. See the examples below.

Sometimes LLMs produce very good work. (For example, if you ask ChatGPT to write
you an implementation of Selection Sort in whatever language, you'll probably get
sensible code.) But sometimes LLMs produce results that are mediocre or nonsensical or
flat-out wrong. It's up to you to determine which you're looking at.

Your goal in this course should be to gain as deep an understanding as possible of
the algorithms, algorithm paradigms, proof techniques, applications, etc. that we will study. If you
find yourself outsourcing the job of understanding to an LLM, then you're not using
this tool effectively and you should talk to me about better ways to use (or not use) LLMs
in your studies.

statements.anchor: Labs have the same AI policy as your lecture section.
statements.label: labs follow lecture AI policy
statements.passage:
Labs have the same AI policy as your lecture section.

Understanding and using AI are important skills that you will master as part of your CS education at Colby, and the following policy will provide a controlled way for you to use AI to your learning advantage in this course:

Students may use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) solely for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback on their code. These tools can be valuable for clarifying ideas and enhancing comprehension.

Using AI to generate any code, solutions, or answers is strictly prohibited and considered academic misconduct. All submitted work must be entirely the student’s own effort.

Students must be able to demonstrate their understanding of solutions through verbal explanations, either in class discussions, office hours, or during assessments.

When AI tools are used for understanding concepts, reviewing examples, or receiving feedback related to a specific assignment or project, students must:

Clearly indicate the extent and nature of the AI’s contribution.

Be prepared to discuss and explain the submitted work during office hours or in class

The use of AI code completion tools, such as GitHub Copilot or other similar platforms, is completely prohibited. Students must write and develop their code independently to ensure they are practicing and reinforcing the skills taught in the course.

Here are some examples of prompts that do not violate the AI policy:

“What is the difference between a stack and a queue?”

“How does a binary search tree work?”

“I'm encountering this error message 'IndexError: list index out of range' when running my code. What does it mean, and how can I fix it?”

“Can you explain how Dijkstra's algorithm works? I'm trying to understand its steps and how it’s applied in practice.”

“Can you help me debug my code? Don't generate any code, just help me understand why my code is not working.”

Here are some examples of prompts that violate the AI policy:

“Can you provide me with a solution to this problem?”

“Can you write a function that ...?”

“Can you generate a code snippet that ....?”

“Can you fix my code so that ...?”

Violations of this policy, including the use of AI for generating code or failure to properly document AI interactions, may result in penalties ranging from a warning to a failing grade for the assignment or course, in accordance with the institution's academic integrity policy.

statements.anchor: I encourage you to use AI in this course to build your proficiency.
statements.label: AI encouraged to build proficiency
statements.passage:
Effective use of AI has become a core skill in modern computer science and related fields. I encourage you to use AI in this course to build your proficiency. However, with freedom comes responsibility: use AI to enhance your learning, not replace it. You must find balance in your usage so that you learn effectively — this looks different for everyone and requires experimentation.

A primary goal of this course is to prepare you as an AI tool builder. That requires hands-on practice with coding, design, and analysis. If AI does that heavy lifting for you, you have gone too far. Here are a few ideas to guide your AI usage:

Code review:
Write a method yourself, then have AI help you check your work. Make sure you understand any suggestions or fixes the AI proposes. Never accept fixes blindly; your solution may be better aligned with the project goals.

Explore alternative implementations:
Ask AI for more readable or efficient implementations. You might learn about an approach that you did not consider!

Mock quizzes:
Have AI quiz you on concepts, code, or results.

Ultimately, you are responsible for all the code and analyses that you turn in; AI cannot take the blame for shortcomings.
Here are several points to keep in mind:

For base projects, you should only use Python packages listed in
Software
. Do not let AI convince you otherwise.

Be cautious of AI suggestions that involve esoteric or exotic functions or overly complex implementations. If you cannot read and understand them, do not include them!
